_note: The air war as its own game (the grand campaign only). Aircraft fly from airfields: places on the map with a size, which engineers can lay out and the treasury can enlarge. Each air fleet history lists is split into air groups of one kind, fighters or bombers, of at most groups.most aircraft. A group patrols, rests, or flies one raid a month. A raid is planned from its target: who can reach it, what will meet it, the chance of success and the losses to expect, and it is flown the moment the order is given.

fields._note: sizes is how many aircraft a seeded airfield serves, by its class: 1 a landing ground, 2 an airfield, 3 an air base. Every level built on top (the arsenal's airfields, or engineers as far as 'engineers') serves arsenal.works.field.holds more. seed says where the war begins with airfields: an air base wherever history bases an air fleet and at every capital, an airfield in every city, a landing ground in every town. least is what a group stranded on bare ground can still fly. words name an airfield from the aircraft it serves.

groups._note: most is the largest group a fleet is split into. names is how each nation numbers its groups of each kind: {n} is the number and {nth} the ordinal. A command small enough to be one group keeps its own name.

raids._note: The kinds of raid the planner offers, in the order shown. needs says which aircraft can fly it at all.

kinds.label: Bomb factories and railways
kinds.blurb: Bombers go for the factories and rail yards of one province by day. Fighters in range can go with them.

kinds.label: Bomb by night
kinds.blurb: Bombers go in darkness with no escort: few are lost, and only about a third of the bombs find the target.

kinds.label: Raid troops
kinds.blurb: Fighters and bombers go for an enemy army where it stands: its organisation is cut for the battle that follows, and some of its men and guns are lost.

kinds.label: Fight for the sky
kinds.blurb: Fighters sweep the sky over one province and bombers hit its airfields. Win it and your armies and fleets have the air there for a month.

kinds.label: Strike shipping
kinds.blurb: Bombers hunt warships and merchant ships in one sea.

kinds.label: Strike a fleet
kinds.blurb: Bombers go for one enemy fleet at sea that your side has found. Carrier aircraft are trained for it; land bombers mostly are not. Its carrier fighters and its guns defend it.

kinds.label: Raid a harbour
kinds.blurb: Bombers go for the warships lying in one harbour. Ships at anchor cannot manoeuvre, and a harbour raided in the month war is declared is caught unready.

kinds.label: Scout from the air
kinds.blurb: A few aircraft photograph one province and the ground round it: every army there is seen whole until the month ends.

ground._note: A raid on troops. intensity is how hard the month's fighting is beside a fight for the sky (1). fighters is what one fighter is worth beside a bomber against troops. The organisation cut is weight / (scale + perDiv x enemy divisions there), never more than max; troops in cover (by terrain) or dug in lose less. str is the share of the cut that is also lost in men and guns. fire is the share of the attacking fighters brought down by ground fire. value is what a point of the cut on one division counts for when the raid is judged.

recon._note: A reconnaissance flight. aircraft is how many of the group go. loss is the share of them lost when enemy fighters patrol the target, per unit of their cover there. ready is the readiness the group spends.

losses._note: What a raid costs in bombers, in the air war. The share lost is bombers x (the defending fighters' share of the fighting weight over the target) to the power 'power', plus what the guns bring down, and never more than most. The escort and the bombers' own guns are the rest of that weight, so an escort saves far more than its numbers. Set against history: a day raid that goes without escort into a strong patrol loses 15 to 25% of its bombers and an escorted one 3 to 8%. By night the few fighters that find the bombers take 2 to 5%. clash is how hard the fighters of the two sides fight over a raid, beside a fight for the sky (1): the escort is there to see the bombers through, not to hunt.

success._note: The chance of success shown before a raid: a raid succeeds when it costs the enemy more than it costs you. k is how sharply the chance turns on the expected exchange. Set from 489 raids flown by four nations over six months: at 12 the raids given 10 to 25% won 15% of the time, those given 25 to 40% won 38%, and those given over 90% all won.

ai._note: The computer's air staff. escortReady is the least readiness at which a fighter group flies escort. raids is how every computer nation at war plans raids of its own, at every level: each month 'share' of its bomber groups fit to fly go out (a group is fit with 'least' bombers and readiness 'ready'), each against the best target among the 'look' most promising it can reach, and only where the forecast gives a chance of success of 'success' or better, a gain of 'worth' aircraft or more, and bomber losses of no more than 'loss'. 'rail' is what a province with a junction and no factory is worth beside one with industry. It flies up to 'sweeps' fights for the sky a month, over front where its fighters go in at 'sky' times the odds that win it; 'skyWorth' is what the sky over an army's front is worth to it, in aircraft. The harder levels replace share, least, loss and rail for a rival (difficulty.json, bombing); the easier ones cut a rival's share.
